lesson.title: Delta-Wye Transformation: Swapping Shapes Without Changing Behavior
lesson.summary: The delta wye transformation gives exact formulas for converting between the two three terminal resistor configurations so a network's external behavior is unchanged, unlocking simplification that plain series and parallel reduction cannot reach on its own.
lesson.body:
The previous two chapters showed, with one specific pair of numbers, that a delta configuration and a wye configuration can be electrically identical at every external terminal. The delta wye transformation turns that observation into exact formulas that work for any set of resistor values, balanced or not. Converting delta resistors R_AB, R_BC, and R_CA into their equivalent wye resistors Ra, Rb, and Rc uses this pattern: each wye resistor equals the product of the two delta resistors that touch its terminal, divided by the sum of all three delta resistors. Written out, Ra = (R_AB times R_CA) divided by (R_AB + R_BC + R_CA), Rb = (R_AB times R_BC) divided by that same sum, and Rc = (R_BC times R_CA) divided by that same sum. The reverse direction, wye to delta, uses R_AB = (Ra Rb + Rb Rc + Rc Ra) divided by Rc, and the other two delta resistors follow the same pattern by rotating which wye resistor sits in the denominator.

The balanced special case is worth memorizing on its own: when all three delta resistors are equal to some value R_delta, every wye resistor comes out equal to R_delta divided by 3, and conversely a balanced wye of R_Y becomes a balanced delta of 3 times R_Y. This matches the earlier chapters exactly: a 30 ohm balanced delta transforms into a 10 ohm balanced wye, and both were shown to produce the same 20 ohm reading between any two terminals.

For the general, unbalanced case, take a delta with R_AB = 6 ohm, R_BC = 12 ohm, and R_CA = 18 ohm. The sum of all three is 6 + 12 + 18 = 36 ohm. The wye resistor at node A, which touches R_AB and R_CA, is (6 times 18) divided by 36, or 108 divided by 36, which is 3 ohm. The wye resistor at node B, which touches R_AB and R_BC, is (6 times 12) divided by 36, or 72 divided by 36, which is 2 ohm. The wye resistor at node C, which touches R_BC and R_CA, is (12 times 18) divided by 36, or 216 divided by 36, which is 6 ohm. So this particular unbalanced delta converts into a wye of 3 ohm, 2 ohm, and 6 ohm at nodes A, B, and C respectively.

It is worth being clear about what this transformation actually guarantees: it does not approximate the original network, it reproduces its behavior exactly at the three terminals involved. Every voltage and current outside those three terminals is completely unaffected by swapping one configuration for the other, only the internal wiring changes. That exactness is precisely why the transformation is useful for simplification rather than just a curiosity: whenever a delta or a wye is buried inside a larger network in a way that blocks ordinary series and parallel reduction, most famously in bridge circuits, converting that one piece unlocks the rest of the reduction.

One quick sanity check worth keeping in your pocket: the units always work out to ohms. Each wye resistor formula is (ohms times ohms) divided by ohms, which leaves ohms, so a units mismatch in your algebra is an immediate sign an arithmetic slip happened somewhere. The 3 ohm, 2 ohm, 6 ohm wye found above will reappear directly in the next chapter, as the key that unlocks a bridge circuit that plain series and parallel reduction cannot touch on its own.
